query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermal aging treatment that promotes the in situ formation of fine, coherent nanoprecipitates in the soft FCC lamellae of a eutectic high‐entropy alloy will simultaneously enhance both strength and ductility compared to the as‐cast microstructure.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting a lamellar microstructure with alternating soft FCC and hard BCC/B2 phases (e.g. AlCoCrFeNi2.1-type alloy).
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled thermal aging procedure (e.g. at 400–600 °C for a calibrated duration under inert atmosphere) to induce the formation of nanometer-scale coherent precipitates within the soft FCC regions.
generation.conditions: Aging treatments should be performed under controlled inert atmosphere conditions (to prevent oxidation) at moderate temperatures (around 400–600 °C) for durations that avoid over-aging, followed by room temperature tensile testing.
generation.structural_mediator: The fine, coherent nanoprecipitates that form within the FCC lamellae serve as internal obstacles to dislocation motion while maintaining coherent interfaces that aid dislocation transmission.
generation.mechanism: The nanoprecipitates act as strong obstacles to dislocation motion, thereby improving strength via precipitation hardening, while their coherent interfaces reduce local stress concentrations and promote dislocation bypass, which mitigates premature failure and enhances ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast eutectic alloy, the aged alloy is expected to show a significant increase in yield strength (tentatively on the order of ~20–30% improvement, though exact numbers remain to be determined) along with improved uniform elongation.
generation.baseline: The as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy that possesses a lamellar FCC/BCC microstructure without intentional aging-induced nanoprecipitation.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to be operative only within an optimal window of aging temperatures and durations. Excessive aging (leading to precipitate coarsening) or temperatures outside the tested range may not yield the desired simultaneous improvement.
generation.uncertainty: The precise aging conditions (temperature and time) and quantitative magnitude of the property improvements require experimental calibration; while prior evidence supports the potential of coherent nanoprecipitates to improve both strength and ductility, the scale of improvement in eutectic HEAs remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of eutectic HEA samples with identical as-cast microstructures. Subject subsets of these samples to different aging treatments (varying temperature within 400–600 °C and aging time) under an inert atmosphere. Assess the microstructure using TEM (to characterize nanoprecipitate size, distribution, and coherence) and perform room-temperature tensile tests to measure yield strength and ductility. Compare results with those of a control (non-aged) sample.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If none of the aging conditions produces a statistically significant simultaneous enhancement (e.g., >15–20% improvement in both yield strength and ductility) over the as-cast baseline, or if the treatment improves strength at the expense of ductility (i.e., ductility decreases), then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.
